items.title: Leadership, burnout, and organizational mental health: a neuroscience-informed perspective
items.abstract: This article argues that the persistent burden of burnout reflects a fundamental conceptual problem—burnout continues to be framed primarily as an individual condition rather than as an occupational phenomenon shaped by interacting structural, organizational, and leadership conditions. Burnout has emerged as a major occupational health challenge. In a 2024 survey across eight predominantly high and upper-middle-income countries, 48% of respondents reported currently grappling with burnout. Separately, depression and anxiety cost the global economy approximately one trillion dollars annually in lost productivity. Drawing on evidence from neuroimaging, stress biology, cognitive neuroscience, and organizational research, this article examines plausible pathways through which leadership behavior may influence conditions that contribute to or protect against burnout, including social threat–reward processing, cognitive flexibility, emotional intelligence, psychological safety, emotional contagion, and stress-related neurobiological responses. Among physicians, burnout has been associated with depression and anxiety, while evidence regarding substance abuse is less consistent. These proposed mechanisms are proximal and potentially modifiable, but operate within broader structural conditions that constrain or enable their effects. Human-centered work design and neuroleadership-informed leadership practices are proposed as complements to broader structural interventions, with implications for health systems, workforce sustainability, and policy design.

items.title: Learning Beyond the Classroom: Examining Achievement and Engagement in Blended Learning Environments
items.abstract: Blended learning, which integrates face-to-face instruction with technology-mediated online components, has gained prominence as schools seek flexible and learner-centred pedagogies. This study examined the effect of a blended learning approach on the academic achievement and classroom engagement of secondary school students in Kerala, India. A quasi-experimental, non-equivalent control group design was employed with 120 ninth-grade students drawn from two comparable government-aided schools. The experimental group (n = 60) received eight weeks of blended instruction combining classroom teaching with a learning management system, interactive video lessons, and online formative quizzes, while the control group (n = 60) received conventional lecture-based instruction. Academic achievement was measured using a validated 40-item subject achievement test administered as pre-test and post-test, and engagement was assessed with a 20-item student engagement scale measuring behavioural, emotional, and cognitive dimensions. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), controlling for pre-test scores, revealed a statistically significant difference in post-test achievement favouring the experimental group (F = 28.64, p < .001), with a large effect size (partial eta squared = .20). The blended learning group also reported significantly higher engagement across all three dimensions, with the largest gain in cognitive engagement. Findings suggest that a well-structured blended approach can enhance both learning outcomes and engagement at the secondary level. The study recommends sustained teacher training in blended pedagogy and improved digital infrastructure, and discusses implications for classroom practice, curriculum design, and education policy.

items.title: Learning to Distrust Correct Answers: The Effect of Deliberate AI-Induced Ambiguity on Conceptual Reasoning in Electrical Engineering Students
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly becoming part of engineering students’ learning environments, particularly in quantitative problem solving, explanation generation, and formative feedback. The educational value of these systems, however, depends not only on output accuracy but also on whether learners can evaluate claims that appear authoritative. This paper proposes Deliberate Ambiguity Verification (DAV), an instructional framework in which electrical engineering students compare two AI-generated solutions that are mathematically plausible and professionally presented but differ in a consequential assumption, boundary condition, or physical interpretation. Students must identify the point of divergence, verify each response against an independent engineering principle, justify a decision, and report confidence before and after verification. The framework integrates epistemic vigilance, trust calibration, metacognitive monitoring, cognitive engagement, productive failure, and discipline-specific AI literacy. A randomized four-condition design is proposed for students in circuit analysis, contrasting no-AI problem solving, a single AI answer, a plausible-but-incorrect AI answer, and deliberate ambiguity. Primary outcomes are conceptual reasoning, verification behavior, confidence calibration, and AI-free transfer. The paper argues that the goal should not be generalized distrust of AI, but calibrated skepticism: the capacity to determine when an AI response should be accepted provisionally, when it requires independent verification, and when disciplinary reasoning should override the apparent authority of the system. The framework is intended to provide a testable pathway for studying epistemically responsible human-AI collaboration in engineering education.

items.title: Making Healthcare AI Explainable: A Structured Review of Methods and Clinical Practice
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming modern medicine, providing powerful tools to assist clinicians. However, the most accurate models are opaque, and their limited interpretability hinders clinical adoption and raises regulatory concerns. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) aims to make these models’ decisions comprehensible. Despite its rapid growth and the many reviews already published, aspects such as the rigor of explanation evaluation, clinician involvement, and the use of large language models to generate explanations appear to have received limited attention. This article is a structured, relevance-prioritized review of XAI applied in healthcare, organized around six research questions covering the XAI techniques used, the data and clinical domains they are paired with, the models they explain, how evaluation is performed, the identified limitations, and the use of large language models. Unlike prior reviews that each address only part of this scope, we bring these dimensions together and quantify how rigorously explanations are evaluated and how often the underlying models are externally validated. We conducted a structured search across four literature sources: IEEE Xplore, PubMed, Google Scholar, and PubMed Central (PMC). We adapted the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flow by carrying a relevance-prioritized subset forward to full-text eligibility assessment, yielding 64 articles for synthesis. Within this corpus, our review revealed a predominantly image-based, post hoc XAI landscape dominated by a few established methods such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), mostly paired with convolutional, tree-based, and hybrid models on classification and risk-prediction tasks. Clinicians evaluated the explanations in only a minority of the included studies, and relatively few models were externally validated, with no evidence of large language models in our corpus. We conclude that stronger evaluation practices and closer collaboration with clinicians are needed to produce models that are clinically useful and safe to deploy.

items.title: Managing the transformation of the cognitive potential of the economy through the introduction of generative AI as a personnel innovation in the face of labor shortages
items.abstract: The problem of structural labor shortages in the digital economy requires the implementation of breakthrough personnel innovations. Generative AI (GAI), which has automation and cognitive augmentation functions, is considered a strategic tool for managing the transformation of cognitive potential and compensating for labor shortages. The lack of quantitative assessment of the scale of labor shortage compensation through the dual effect (replacement and augmentation) of GAI in key sectors of the economy and the need to verify the strategic role of GAI as a personnel innovation are driving research on this issue. An assessment was conducted of the management of the transformation of the economy’s cognitive potential through the introduction of AI as a personnel innovation in conditions of a labour shortage. A comprehensive approach was applied, combining general scientific methods, statistical analysis, and economic mathematical modelling. The overall compensation of cognitive load through the implementation of generative AI in trade, manufacturing, and professional activities will amount to 5.752 million people in terms of headcount equivalent by 2027, which is more than four times the projected need to compensate for the structural deficit (1.4 million people). Generative AI acts not only as a means of covering the staffing deficit but also as a tool for the qualitative transformation of the economy’s cognitive potential, shifting the focus of employment to hybrid jobs and tasks that require a “human core” of competencies. For the first time, the concept of the “cognitive substitutability coefficient of GAI” (λGAI) has been proposed within the framework of the model of cognitive transformation of labor resources to quantitatively assess the total compensatory effect (automation + augmentation) of implementing GAI in the economy.

items.title: Mechanistic Interpretability and Explainable AI (XAI) in Foundation Models: Reverse-Engineering Circuits, Superposition, and Safety Bounds
items.abstract: Abstract—Foundation models, particularly autoregressive Transformer Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), have exhibited unprecedented reasoning and generative capabilities across computer science and engineering. However, their internal representations operate as opaque, high-dimensional 'black boxes.' Conventional Explainable AI (XAI) techniques—predominantly post-hoc attribution methods such as Integrated Gradients, SHAP, and attention heatmap visualizations—fail to provide faithful causal explanations: they reflect output correlations rather than the internal mechanistic computations executing within the network, masking hazardous failure modes like latent hallucinations, sycophancy, and deceptive alignment. Mechanistic Interpretability has emerged as a rigorous bottom-up paradigm that seeks to reverse-engineer deep neural networks into human-understandable algorithmic circuits, decomposing polysemantic neuron activations into monosemantic features. This paper provides an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation of mechanistic interpretability and XAI for modern foundation models. We formalize the Linear Representation Hypothesis and the mathematics of neural superposition, analyze transformer residual streams as communicative communication buses, and model the discovery of specialized functional subgraphs—including induction heads, factual recall circuits, and indirect object identification (IOI) subnetworks. Furthermore, we evaluate Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) as an unsupervised mechanism to disentangle polysemantic latent spaces into overcomplete, monosemantic feature dictionaries. Finally, we implement an empirical evaluation testbed across open foundation models (Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B, and Mistral-7B), quantitatively benchmarking causal scrubbing, activation patching, and SAE feature steering across mission-critical tasks (deceptive alignment detection, factual hallucination suppression, and jailbreak defense). Our findings demonstrate that activation patching isolates causal circuits responsible for 92.4% of factual routing, while SAE-guided feature clamping suppresses unfaithful hallucinations by 41.7% with less than 2.1% degradation in baseline perplexity. We conclude by formulating open challenges in circuit universality, superposition scaling laws, and regulatory verification under international AI governance frameworks. Index Terms—Mechanistic Interpretability, Explainable AI (XAI), Foundation Models, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), Polysemanticity, Neural Superposition, Induction Heads, Activation Patching, Transformer Circuits.

items.title: Mobile Generative AI Literacy and English Writing Self-Efficacy: The Role of AI Feedback Engagement in Higher Education
items.abstract: This study examines the relationship between mobile Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) literacy and English writing self-efficacy (EWSE) among university students, with AI feedback engagement (AFE) proposed as a mediating mechanism. Using a quantitative cross-sectional design, data were collected from 312 university students in China through validated self-report measures. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was employed to test the proposed relationships and mediation effects. The results show that mobile GenAI literacy (MGL) significantly predicts AFE (β = 0.563, p < 0.001) and EWSE (β = 0.182, p = 0.003), while AFE significantly predicts writing self-efficacy (β = 0.478, p < 0.001). AFE partially mediates the relationship between MGL and writing self-efficacy, accounting for approximately 59.6% of the total effect. The model explains 41.2% of the variance in writing self-efficacy. These findings indicate that the educational value of MGL extends beyond technological competence, with active engagement in AI-generated feedback serving as an important mechanism for strengthening writing confidence. The study highlights the importance of pedagogical approaches that promote critical evaluation, reflective use, and meaningful engagement with AI feedback.

items.title: Network Topology Shapes AI Intervention Effectiveness on Deception: Truth-Telling vs. Investigative Agents
items.abstract: Deploying AI agents to combat dishonest communication is an intuitive response to deception in hybrid human-AI societies. However, the efficacy of such interventions in realistic networked settings remains unclear. We study this problem using an evolutionary game-theoretic model of the Deceiver's Game by extending it to structured networks, where agents can adopt deception, truth-telling, and investigation strategies. We introduce committed AI agents (zealots) fixed to either truth-telling or investigative strategies and conduct agent-based simulations across three network topologies. Our key findings are: (1) passive committed truth-telling agents can amplify adaptive deception by creating exploitable honest partners, whereas investigative agents increase adaptive truth-telling in the oscillatory regime; (2) intervention effects are non-monotonic in deployment density because committed agents reshape rather than simply suppress the underlying oscillatory dynamics; and (3) response peaks depend on topology, with sampled scale-free populations showing sharp low-density responses and fully connected populations requiring larger committed fractions. Overall, the results highlight the need to distinguish passive truth-telling from active investigation when using committed agents to influence networked deception dynamics.

items.title: One AI Approval Is Not Unlimited Authority: Reality-Gated Execution for Frontier AI and Critical Systems
items.abstract: An AI agent receives permission to execute a command. But what if the command reaches the wrong destination, the payment follows a compromised route, or a robotic actuator behaves differently from what was authorized? Should that original permission still allow the system to continue? As frontier AI models and autonomous agents increasingly control financial transactions, cloud infrastructure, sensitive communications, software deployments, industrial equipment, robotics, and critical systems, conventional authorization faces a fundamental limitation: permission to execute does not establish that the intended real-world effect actually occurred. This paper examines a different approach to machine authority: “A permit to effect once is not a permit to effect permanently.” Building on the principle that “Computation is not authority to act,” the proposed architecture introduces a further requirement: authority to continue must be earned through independently verified evidence of a preceding real effect. The paper presents a safety-first execution-finality architecture based on Receipt-Gated Interim Effectuation Validation (IEV). Instead of immediately releasing the full consequence of a high-risk operation, the system can authorize a deliberately bounded real effect on the actual operational path. A protected observer, destination, transaction system, network component, or hardware controller produces evidence of what actually occurred. An independent Interim Effectuation Validator examines that evidence against the authorized act, expected outcome, destination, scope, freshness, policy, and revocation state. Only successful validation establishes the protected continuation condition required for the next phase. In stronger realizations, this is not merely another software approval. The cryptographic material required to complete the next effect is unavailable until the preceding real-world effect has been independently verified. Continuation may depend on receipt-bound key derivation, split credentials, protected state transitions, threshold approvals, hardware registers, or other protected enforcement mechanisms. The validator does not relay the original command, and an agent's own assertion of success is never a substitute for required independent evidence. The paper consolidates 35 execution-finality workflow profiles (E01–E35) spanning eight broad technical families, including: AI agents, autonomous tool execution, frontier model deployment, and credential control. Financial transactions, payment verification, settlement, and protected value release. Messages, file transfers, confidential data disclosure, and destination verification. Cloud infrastructure, database mutations, software updates, and persistent AI memory. Robotics, industrial automation, autonomous vehicles, and unmanned aerial systems. Telecommunications, radio transmission, satellite operations, and network control. GPUs, accelerators, hardware enforcement, and protected execution domains. Distributed effectuation, quorum validation, uncertain outcomes, and recovery. The architecture also examines 12 implementation-equivalence and design-around closures, addressing attempts to bypass the protected causal dependency through alternate execution paths, substituted components, software–hardware rearrangements, or different credential and validation topologies. A dedicated Safety-First Critical-System Profile establishes that execution correctness, consequence containment, and mandatory validation take precedence over minimizing latency. Optimizations remain possible, but they must preserve the protections selected for the relevant consequence class. A further distinction is made between simulation and actual effectuation. A successful simulation cannot establish that the real recipient, network route, transaction destination, or physical actuator will behave as expected. The proposed staged mechanism therefore uses bounded effects on the actual consequence-capable path, subject to protected observation and explicit safety assumptions. When evidence is missing, conflicting, stale, replayed, or indeterminate, ordinary continuation remains unavailable. Unknown outcomes require reconciliation, bounded remediation, safe-state handling, or protected escalation—not automatic success or blind retry. The central research question is straightforward: Should a high-consequence autonomous machine be permitted to cause its next irreversible effect before independently verifying what happened during its previous authorized effect? This publication proposes that, for selected high-risk operations, real-world evidence should become a technical and cryptographic prerequisite for continuing execution—not merely an audit record produced after the consequences have occurred. The paper is a technical architecture and analytical contribution. It does not report experimental deployment, measured security improvements, or empirical validation. Its proposed properties depend on assumptions concerning evidence integrity, protected authority, enforcement-path completeness, and atomic consumption of continuation authority. Patent pending: Indian Patent Office application 202631117633, “Systems and Methods for Cryptographically Staged Effectuation with Verified Partial Effect, Receipt-Bound Full Effectuation, and Software-Hardware Enforcement.” This publication makes no assertion that any particular commercial system implements the architecture and does not establish patentability, infringement, ownership, or priority. Invitation for Independent Technical Review Researchers, frontier AI model providers, cloud and hardware engineers, security architects, patent professionals, and critical-infrastructure specialists are invited to examine the 35 workflows, test the security assumptions, identify relevant prior art, challenge the anti-bypass properties, and evaluate whether receipt-dependent execution authority provides meaningful additional protection for consequential autonomous systems. Critical feedback, adversarial analysis, alternative engineering approaches, and independent conclusions are welcome.

items.title: Organizational Ergonomics in Robotics
items.abstract: The chapter introduces the organizational dimension of ergonomics for robotics. Specifically, it introduces the foundations of organizational ergonomics and sociotechnical principles for effective work systems design and development. It then highlights key challenges involved in issues related to work, activities, and quality of life in robotic setups. In this realm, attitudes towards robots and automation play a major role in the adoption of new technologies and change management in organizations. These broad-scale changes are important to be recognized as they shape human–robot interaction in various work settings, ranging from smart manufacturing to defence. The chapter then addresses specific aspects of teamwork and the design of high-performance teams. These topics include team performance and well-being, human function allocation, shared situation awareness, and job roles, amongst other such topics that will be explored later in the book by subsequent chapters. This chapter supplements the previous chapters on physical and cognitive ergonomics, but it goes beyond these aspects to highlight the organizational basis required to develop robotics holistically.

items.title: PENGARUH MODEL PEMBELAJARAN SAVI (SOMATIC, AUDIOTORY, VISUALIZATION AND INTELECTUALLY) UNTUK MENINGKATKAN HASIL BELAJAR SISWA
items.abstract: Physical Education, Health, and Sport (PJOK) learning outcomes in elementary schools frequently remain suboptimal due to conventional instructional methods that fail to engage multiple sensory modalities. This empirical gap is evident in students' low mastery of flexibility movement concepts, where varied learning preferences are rarely facilitated simultaneously. Consequently, adopting an integrated learning model that synthesizes bodily movement with cognitive engagement is critical. This study aims to determine the effect of the SAVI (Somatic, Auditory, Visualization, and Intellectually) learning model on fourth-grade students' PJOK learning outcomes at SD Negeri 068332 Simalingkar during the 2025/2026 academic year. A quantitative pre-experimental method with a one-group pretest-posttest design was conducted on 30 students selected via total sampling. Data were gathered through expert-validated achievement tests and student response questionnaires. Findings revealed that the initial pretest average of 50.66 significantly increased to 78.50 in the posttest assessment. The paired sample t-test generated a t_"value" greater than the critical t_"table" (9.859≥1.697) at a significance level of 0.000 (p<0.05). Thus, the SAVI learning model exerts a statistically significant positive effect on enhancing primary students' physical education outcomes. ABSTRAK Hasil belajar Pendidikan Jasmani, Olahraga, dan Kesehatan (PJOK) di sekolah dasar sering kali belum mencapai ketuntasan optimal karena dominasi pembelajaran konvensional yang kurang mengintegrasikan seluruh modalitas sensori siswa. Kesenjangan ini tampak pada rendahnya pemahaman konsep serta keterampilan gerak materi kelenturan yang belum mengakomodasi keberagaman gaya belajar anak secara simultan. Oleh karena itu, penerapan model pembelajaran terpadu yang memadukan aktivitas fisik dan proses berpikir menjadi sangat penting untuk diterapkan. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menguji pengaruh model pembelajaran SAVI (Somatic, Auditory, Visualization, and Intellectually) terhadap peningkatan hasil belajar PJOK siswa kelas IV SD Negeri 068332 Simalingkar Tahun Pembelajaran 2025/2026. Pendekatan kuantitatif dengan desain pre-experimental tipe one-group pretest-posttest design diterapkan terhadap 30 siswa yang dipilih melalui teknik total sampling. Pengumpulan data menggunakan instrumen tes hasil belajar kognitif dan psikomotorik yang telah divalidasi ahli serta angket respon siswa. Hasil penelitian membuktikan bahwa rata-rata pretest sebesar 50,66 meningkat secara signifikan menjadi 78,50 pada perolehan posttest. Hasil analisis uji hipotesis menunjukkan nilai t_"hitung" lebih besar daripada t_"tabel" (9,859≥1,697) dengan signifikansi 0,000 (p<0,05). Dengan demikian, model pembelajaran SAVI berpengaruh signifikan dalam meningkatkan hasil belajar PJOK materi kelenturan pada siswa sekolah dasar.

items.title: Peran Talenta Kecerdasan Buatan dalam Membangun Keunggulan Kompetitif
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed organizational processes and increased the demand for talent with specialized knowledge and skills to integrate AI into business activities. This study aims to examine the role of artificial intelligence talent in building organizational competitive advantage. The research employs a systematic literature review (SLR) by identifying, evaluating, and synthesizing relevant national and international studies on AI talent, AI skills, human capital, innovation, organizational performance, and competitive advantage. The findings indicate that AI talent contributes to competitive advantage through innovation, productivity improvement, data-driven decision-making, knowledge utilization, and organizational AI capabilities. Furthermore, AI talent requires not only technical expertise but also analytical, collaborative, and business-oriented competencies. Theoretically, this study positions AI talent as a strategic human capital resource within the Resource-Based View and Dynamic Capabilities perspectives. Practically, the findings emphasize the importance of strategic recruitment, continuous upskilling and reskilling, and knowledge sharing to optimize AI talent. Overall, AI talent plays an important role in transforming technological capabilities into sustainable competitive advantage.

items.title: Perceived AI support and work outcomes: testing the mediating role of job crafting in AI-supported work
items.abstract: Introduction Organizations increasingly adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI) to gain competitive advantages, but anticipated benefits may not materialize when employee needs and work design aspects are neglected. Job crafting—employees' self-initiated work adjustments—may represent an important mechanism linking perceived AI support with work outcomes, but its role in the context of AI-supported work remains underexplored. Drawing on job demands-resources theory, this cross-sectional study examines relationships between perceived AI support, approach and avoidance crafting, and how these pathways may mediate associations with job satisfaction, perceived productivity, work engagement, turnover intentions, and burnout. Methods Data were collected via an online survey of employees engaged in information and knowledge work in Germany, who use AI systems ( n = 695). Using structural equation modeling, a mediation model with approach and avoidance crafting as parallel mediators was tested. Results Results revealed that perceived AI support was positively associated with both approach and avoidance crafting. Approach crafting emerged as a dominant pathway, being positively associated with job satisfaction, work engagement, and perceived productivity and negatively associated with burnout and turnover intentions. Avoidance crafting showed contrary associations. Total effects of AI support through approach and avoidance crafting indicated associations with increased job satisfaction, perceived productivity and work engagement, and reduced burnout. Discussion These findings extend job crafting theory to AI-supported work by indicating that perceived AI support functions as a job resource that is associated with distinct crafting pathways. Organizations should implement AI systems that employees perceive as supportive, thereby providing a resource that enables job crafting, and further promote approach over avoidance crafting through corresponding work design measures and targeted personnel development.

items.title: Physical Ergonomics in Robotics
items.abstract: With the emergence of embodied intelligent systems like collaborative robots (cobots), the landscape of physically demanding work is changing. Indeed, robotic devices can augment human strength, optimize performance, and minimize the physical demands associated with a job or a task. These achievements of human-robot interaction (HRI) surely match the objectives of physical ergonomics: making physical interactions between humans and other elements of a system more efficient, more gratifying, and safer. One of the key goals of physical ergonomics certainly is to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs). Therefore, a cobot must have insight into the effect of physical stress on the human body. One of the most common ways to provide that is to use the established ergonomics look-up tables that indicate which working configurations and conditions may cause WMSDs based on experience. Another approach is to use musculoskeletal models to get real-time estimates of key internal body parameters, such as joint torques, muscle forces, and muscle fatigue. A cobotic or, in general, robotic system can then use these ergonomic indexes and variables to guide a human co-worker to more favourable configurations and conditions. In this chapter, we examine physical human-robot interactions (pHRIs) to have an introductory overview of possible scenarios and constraints. We then look into the fundamentals of physical ergonomics such as anthropometry, biomechanics, and environmental factors, including important ergonomic assessment tools and innovative indicators developed in robotics. Subsequently, concrete examples of methods that address physical ergonomics with collaborative robotics are examined in terms of design and control methods.

items.title: Quantifying the Subjective Experience in Human–Robot Interaction
items.abstract: Assessing the quality of interaction between collaborative robots (i.e., cobots) and humans to achieve a (shared) goal is an essential part of supporting the diffusion of usable and safe collaborative robotic systems. The key issue here is that cobots within and between domains can vary substantially in terms of features even when these are meant to support similar tasks. Under this perspective, it seems very hard, if not impossible, to identify coherent ways to benchmark the quality of cobots. However, all the cobots share one element which is that they have to deal with humans and satisfy them. This chapter claims that focusing on how a system can satisfy the human counterpart can (indirectly) provide insights into the quality of cobots that can be a piece of valuable information for the designers. In this sense, identifying and validating a set of key aspects to assess the subjective experience in interaction with robots during collaborative tasks is a stepping stone for benchmarking cobots. We will discuss how, in other domains, researchers developed standardized scales to ensure comparable results regarding the user experience (UX), and to model the differences between systems. Moreover, based on a recent systematic literature review, an initial list of key aspects to evaluate UX with cobots is discussed as a step to build and validate a future tool for unifying how experts evaluate cobots.

items.title: Receipts Over Genius: An Audited Account of an 18-Month, AI-Assisted, Solo Invention Cycle
items.abstract: SQUIRL OS RESEARCH DISCLOSURE - READ FIRST: This work is part of an open-book, AI-assisted research program produced under bifurcated governance (a probabilistic AI agent drafts; a deterministic human key approves; a boundary-layer audit checks claims against receipt archives). Audit-and-correction is doctrine: superseded originals are preserved in version histories, corrections are disclosed amendments, and every significant test carries a preregistered falsifier in the append-only public ledger (github.com/LLong2026/four-horsemen). This software and its accompanying research are prototypes provided for educational and research purposes only; they are not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. In April 2025 the author, a working technologist with no background in AI, set himself a falsifiable experiment: use AI assistance to travel the complete invention cycle - conceive, develop the mathematics, build the working system, file the patents, publish the science, demonstrate the result - with every significant step verified by a timestamped, publicly inspectable receipt. This paper is the closing account of that experiment, written under the same rules it describes. Result, scoped honestly: in 18 months a single operator completed the cycle - eight U.S. provisional patent applications pending; a working self-healing infrastructure platform across a live app fleet; the first documented caging of an LLM inside a deterministic mathematical boundary (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23265723), a receipt that survived direct third-party scrutiny; and a public research line (the DCAI community) walking from theory to governance proof to field event. Two findings carry the paper: (1) the experiment succeeded because of the boundary, not despite it - bifurcated governance turned the operator's lack of background into an auditable process; (2) the program generated its own counter-evidence, reported here rather than discarded: five cataloged instances of AI confabulation inside the program itself (fabricated statuses, fabricated evaluation data, a fabricated institutional identity), every one caught by the same receipt discipline the experiment was testing. The method worked on its author's own tooling. Thesis community: Deterministic Caged AI (DCAI) - https://zenodo.org/communities/dcai. Lineage acknowledged: Nyquist (1924), Hartley (1928), Shannon (1948), Kolmogorov (1965), Popper (1959). Companion paper: Deterministic Caging of Probabilistic Large Language Models (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23266727).

items.title: Reference-Assisted Decoding of Sparse Tactile Codes Through Active Sequential Exploration: Time Costs and Similarity-Driven Errors in a Low-Resolution Vibrotactile Interface
items.abstract: Low-resolution tactile interfaces often require users to identify spatial codes through active sequential exploration, but the interaction costs and error structures of reference-assisted sparse-code decoding remain undercharacterized. We studied how 15 novice users decoded Braille-like alphabetic patterns on a 3 × 2 vibrotactile interface using blindfolded tactile exploration followed by visual reference-chart consultation. Participants completed a baseline single-location discrimination task and a three-block character-decoding task without explicit letter-pattern training or trial-wise correctness feedback. Single-location performance was near ceiling, whereas character-decoding accuracy increased across blocks. Exploration accounted for the larger share of task time, but incorrect trials showed a disproportionate prolongation of the composite post-exploration reference-assisted stage. Errors were structured by pattern similarity: most occurred between patterns separated by a Hamming distance of 1, and higher dot counts were associated with lower accuracy and longer response times. These findings inform low-resolution vibrotactile interface design by characterizing interaction costs and pattern confusability.

items.title: Reframing Authorship and Ethics in AI-driven and Immersive Architectural Environments: A Transdisciplinary Review
items.abstract: This article presents a comprehensive transdisciplinary review of the ways in which artificial intelligence(AI) and immersive technologies are transforming foundational concepts of authorship, ethics, and creativitywithin contemporary architecture and spatial design. The traditional notion of the architect as a singular,authoritative creator increasingly is challenged by computational processes that introduce generative, autonomous,and distributed forms of design agency. Through a synthesis of architectural theory, AI ethics, media studies,and posthuman philosophy, the review interrogates the shifting locus of authorship in design environmentsmediated by intelligent systems and extended reality (XR) platforms. At the core of this inquiry is an ontological reframing of authorship, informed by scholars such as RosiBraidotti, Tony Fry, Humberto Maturana, and Anne-Marie Willis. These frameworks position the architect notas an originator of form, but as a participant in a relational field of human and non-human agents, includingalgorithms, data, environments, and users. Adopting an ontological design lens, under which design practicesand their tools co‑produce forms of life and ways of world‑making, the article argues that AI/XR systems donot merely assist representation but actively configure professional authorship, agency, and ethics. This framinglinks practical workflows to normative guidance for disclosure, responsibility, and education. The review exploreshow generative design, neural networks, and parametric modeling redefine design intention and originality,situating authorship as a curatorial and computationally entangled process. In parallel, immersive media suchas virtual and augmented reality introduce new forms of user co-authorship and spatial manipulation, promptingethical questions about consent, agency, presence, and the authenticity of digital space. The article maps emerging discourses around design accountability, legal attribution, algorithmic bias, anddata governance, proposing an expanded ethical vocabulary for posthuman design practices. Through a criticalexamination of scholarly literature, experimental studios, and case-based applications, the review identifiesepistemological and practical challenges in reconciling human-centered traditions with distributed technologicalagency. Ultimately, this article argues for a redefinition of authorship as a dynamic, ethically situated, andontologically pluralistic concept in architecture. It advocates for the development of integrative frameworksthat embed ethical foresight and philosophical reflexivity into AI-augmented and immersive design methodologies.By repositioning the architect as a negotiator within hybrid systems of creativity and control, the articlecontributes a forward-looking perspective to architectural theory, technological practice, and planning discourse.

items.title: RegulaTutor: A Theory-Informed Framework for Long-Term Personalized Learning
items.abstract: Long-term personalized tutoring requires language models to translate a learner's evolving history into appropriate instructional support. Existing LLM-based tutoring systems use memory and retrieval to personalize responses, but the pedagogical rationale linking historical evidence to teaching strategies is not always explicit. We introduce RegulaTutor, a theory-informed framework for long-term personalized tutoring that connects historical evidence, learner interpretation, and learner-facing instruction. Guided by self-regulated learning (SRL) research, its tutoring harness operationalizes a cognitive, affective, metacognitive, and motivational (CAMM) framework for deriving evidence-supported learner interpretations and teaching policies. The resulting policies retain links to their supporting evidence and are updated as new observations arrive. This staged workflow also supports systematic refinement through PairRoute, an offline procedure that uses intermediate execution records to distinguish harness, model, and mixed failures. PairRoute proposes and evaluates targeted harness revisions, then constructs reviewed stage-level supervision for confirmed model failures remaining under the selected harness. We focus this refinement on historical evidence acquisition, which underpins personalized instruction and allows outputs to be checked against learning records and reference answers. RegulaTutor improves historical-evidence accuracy, learner diagnosis, and judged teaching quality on average across evaluated model configurations. PairRoute results show an endpoint improvement in standalone-model historical-evidence accuracy over the refinement trajectory. Together, these results highlight RegulaTutor's potential to support lifelong personalized education through instructional policies that evolve with learner histories and targeted improvements to the tutoring system.

items.title: Relational Role Attribution: A Unifying Construct in Human–AI Interaction
items.abstract: How users come to perceive an AI not merely as capable but as intentionally oriented toward them in a specific relational capacity remains undertheorized. We propose relational role attribution (RRA) as a discrete psychological construct addressing this gap, positioned as a precursor to downstream relational outcomes rather than a reframing of trust. A PRISMA-ScR scoping review charted 1223 reports at full text against a registered protocol, including 466. Of 179 records excluded for establishing no relational or social role for the agent, 122 (68.2%) nonetheless manipulated or measured anthropomorphism: the field reaches the cue and stops short of the attribution. RRA comprises two concurrent components, a relational inference of social orientation and a role assignment drawn from contextual and communicative cues, checked against the expectancy the user brings. Naming the attribution allows findings accumulated separately across marketing, teaming, and communication literatures to constrain one another, and scaffolds role-specific design principles.

items.title: Responsibility closure in healthcare shift handover: A systematic review and SEIPS 2.0-informed framework synthesis
items.abstract: • Responsibility closure shifts handover assessment to each unfinished obligation. • Five conditions distinguish nominal transfer from executable continuity. • Communication improvements often outpace evidence on follow-through and safety. • Work-system capacity is part of credible responsibility transfer. • The framework is provisional and requires prospective validation. Healthcare shift handovers are commonly evaluated as information-transfer events, yet patient safety also depends on whether unfinished work is understood, assigned and executable within the receiving system. We systematically reviewed empirical studies of real healthcare shift-boundary handovers and developed a provisional SEIPS 2.0-informed integrative framework for analysing this operational endpoint. PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection and OpenAlex were searched through 13 July 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching. Screening, eligibility assessment, extraction, MMAT appraisal and synthesis were conducted by the primary reviewer, with independent verification of prespecified samples across review stages. From 2,876 identified records, 172 reports representing 167 independent studies were included. Best-fit framework synthesis identified five analytically distinguishable conditions relevant to credible responsibility closure: visibility of unfinished work; active reception and shared understanding; actionability and priority; explicit ownership; and operational capacity. Intervention studies more consistently reported improvements in communication completeness and documentation, whereas ownership, subsequent action and patient-safety outcomes were less frequently and less robustly evaluated. Responsibility closure describes the obligation-level state in which consequential unfinished work has an identifiable receiving location, a feasible next action and sufficient capacity for action or escalation. It therefore extends beyond information completeness or nominal transfer of accountability by requiring operational executability. The evidence was heterogeneous, predominantly healthcare-based and did not directly validate the construct or its candidate indicators. Responsibility closure offers a provisional systems-oriented framework for designing and evaluating handovers around the continuation of unfinished work. Prospective studies should test its association with follow-through, delay, escalation and harm.

items.title: Robotics for Aging Populations
items.abstract: Robotics offers versatile tools to face the challenges due to the older population growth, especially meeting the needs for assisting the elderly in the activities of daily living (ADLs) and for the geriatric care. However, the perspectives offered by human factors studies can further enhance this potential of robotics. This chapter explores the integration of ergonomics in the design of robots devised to enhance the independence and well-being of older adults. Furthermore, we mention the opportunities offered by wearable robotics, telepresence, and the pervasive solutions of the Internet of Robotic Things (IoRT) to implement paradigms of precision healthcare with decentralized and ubiquitous features, improving the sustainability of elderly care—following the human-centric perspectives of Society 5.0 and Health 5.0, with their synergies. For instance, we discuss issues of technology acceptance alongside the perspectives of value-sensitive design to ensure that robotics align with the experiential and, in particular, ethical needs in aging people and communities, first of all for inclusion. Intelligent systems will also be discussed for their potential to make robotic solutions even more versatile and adjustable to the seniors’ needs. By prioritizing the needs and preferences of older individuals (and their own network of relatives, friends, and acquaintances), ergonomics in robotics must contribute to the societal mission of preserving dignity, autonomy, and quality of life in aging societies.

items.title: Sapiens in Control: A Six-Dimension Framework for Evaluating Control Failures in Advanced AI Agents
items.abstract: Sapiens in Control, formerly Human in Control, proposes a six-dimension Human Control Model for reviewing control failures in advanced AI agents. It distinguishes real-world incidents, mixed or contained events, controlled evaluations, and simulations. Version 1.4 builds on v1.3.1 and adds bounded analysis of METR's October 6 transcript-viewer proof of concept and OpenAI's October 6 metagaming research. It proposes separate oversight checks for authoritative records, displayed or exported evidence, reasoning traces, actions, and independently observed outcomes. These are research examples and evaluation proposals, not additional confirmed deployment incidents or completed validation. The six dimensions, five pilot cases, qualitative severity definitions, and prior corrections are preserved. This remains an unreviewed conceptual working paper without completed independent reliability testing. AI tools assisted drafting, source review, and document preparation; this revision is not peer review or private-log verification.

items.title: Second-Generation AI: The Hybrid Survivability Criterion. Open specification, version 0.2 / ИИ второго поколения: критерий гибридной выживаемости
items.abstract: An open specification proposing that a generation of AI be defined not by a model's power or speed, but by the hybrid survivability of the human operator and the machine as a single system: its harmlessness in three circles — for the operator, for the people around while it works, and for the people affected by the outcome. It starts from the nature of hybrid text: written by creators of different natures who seem to speak one language, instrumental, fast to synthesize, scalable, and contagious for people and for the next AI models. First generation extends human capabilities; second generation extends and protects. The specification distinguishes system outcome from the contribution of model training, lists eight functions of a second-generation model, a signature threshold for hybrid texts, a two-stage evaluation design with a severity scale, and the closest prior work. Companion to the essay "The Second Generation of AI". English and Russian versions. Written with the participation of AI (Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek).

items.title: Self-Reflection and Error-Correction Mechanisms in LLMs Driven by Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Large language models have shown very strong abilities on complex reason work, but they still have many problems, these problems include error accumulation and hallucinations. Therefore, letting these models have the ability of self-reflection and error correction has hence become a core research focus. This research puts focus on the self-reflection mechanisms which are pushed forward by reinforcement learning, and it carries out a systematic review on representative research work in this domain. The covering scope contains emergent thinking manifestation, clear teaching practice, many-circle improvement, multi-angle comment, many-intelligence cooperation, and changeable framework designs. Comparison analysis makes clear that reinforcement learning optimizes the decision-making policy through balancing gradient attribution, hence supervised fine-tuning is easy to appear behavioral collapse and distribution shift. The ability of reflection may either come forth in the process of RL training, or be explicitly constructed as a module that can be learned. The research work that will be done in future therefore needs to carry out further exploration on the interpretability of reflection, the design of reward, and the transferability across different tasks. This research offers a systematic theory frame and practical direction for the comprehension and building of self-correcting LLMs.

items.title: Shared Control for Assistive and Collaborative Robotics
items.abstract: Assistive and collaborative robots offer a promising solution for reducing human physical stress and exposure across a broad range of applications. The design and control of such robotic systems should account for humans needs, so as to assist their motion and activity as well as optimize their efficiency and performance throughout the considered tasks. In this respect, designing around the human means accounting for their musculoskeletal constraints, features, and limitations during the development of robotic mechanical systems and control algorithms, such as powered exoskeletons or cobots. This Chapter presents an overview of human-centered design and shared control techniques in robotics, including supporting examples and applications in the field of industrial teleoperation and mobility assistance. We also discuss the perspectives of the field and how such human-centered approaches can be beneficial to a broader range of applications than those where it is implemented nowadays.

items.title: Shipboard Conflict, Maritime Safety and Human Factors: Toward A Socio-Technical Theory of Conflict in Multicultural and Digital Shipping
items.abstract: Abstract Contemporary shipping operates through the interaction of sophisticated technologies, multinational crews, hierarchical authority and employment relations within safety-critical environments. Maritime safety research has established the importance of fatigue, workload, communication, situational awareness, human error, organisational conditions and cultural diversity. Recent studies have also begun to model conflict alongside language and communication factors in maritime risk. The unresolved theoretical question is therefore not whether conflict matters, but whether persistent and unresolved safety-relevant shipboard conflict constitutes a distinct relational mechanism with explanatory value beyond established human-factor constructs. This conceptual paper develops Conflict-Induced Maritime Risk Theory (CIMRT) to address that question. CIMRT proposes that organisational, employment-relational, cultural and technological conditions can influence the emergence and persistence of unresolved conflict, which may subsequently affect human-factor coordination and safety-related behaviour. Socio-Technical Systems Theory provides the principal theoretical foundation, complemented by Social Identity Theory, Crew Resource Management, Safety Culture, Human Factors Analysis and Classification System, and Resilience Engineering. The paper does not claim empirical validation. Instead, it specifies a staged research programme involving construct development, expert assessment, cognitive interviewing, factor validation, structural modelling, qualitative inquiry and comparative model testing. Particular emphasis is placed on distinguishing conflict from frustration, communication quality, workload, fatigue, organisational injustice and psychological unsafety. CIMRT is consequently advanced as a falsifiable theoretical proposition. Its contribution will depend on whether unresolved safety-relevant conflict can demonstrate conceptual distinctiveness, plausible temporal ordering and meaningful incremental explanatory value beyond established maritime safety explanations. Keywords: Shipboard conflict; Maritime safety; Human factors; Multicultural crews; Sociotechnical systems; Digital shipping

items.abstract: This chapter explores the ergonomic, cognitive, and psychological mechanisms underpinning human–robot communication, focusing on the role of social robots in shaping human perception, behaviour, and socio-emotional engagement. By analysing factors such as robot design, embodiment, and communication modalities, the chapter highlights how these elements influence user interaction and the perception of robots as social entities. It examines the integration of verbal and non-verbal communication modalities, addressing challenges in reciprocity and robots’ behavioural appropriateness. The discussion extends to the implications of adaptive technologies like large language models, emphasising the balance between responsiveness and confidentiality in human–robot interactions. Furthermore, the chapter underscores the potential of social robots in workplace and therapeutic settings to enhance efficiency, safety, and emotional well-being of human interactants. By addressing user expectations and ethical considerations, the chapter seeks to provide a comprehensive framework for advancing social robotics applications in fostering meaningful human–robot relationships.

items.title: Surrendering Consumption to Artificial Intelligence: Consumer Agency and Responsible Consumption in AI-Mediated Markets
items.abstract: This paper explores the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in shaping consumption, and the contribution AI might make to transitioning to a responsible consumption and production regime, in line with Goal 12 of the UN Sustainable Development Goals. This paper draws on Practice Theory, an established framework for studying sustainable consumption practices. Based on this framework, the authors suggest that whilst in traditional consumption, the expertise required to consume resides in human subjects, in AI-shaped consumption this expertise resides in AI algorithms. This may have implications for consumers’ agency and can put them at disadvantage. Indeed, the EU has proposed regulations to control the use of AI by providers. The paper draws on two case studies, Ant Forest, a Chinese app which prompts consumers to adopt responsible consumption practices and Mobility as a Service, a platform-based mobility offering. We find that whilst the former contributes to establishing consumers’ expertise in sustainable behavior—for example, through gaming—the latter may remove consumers’ choice by performing some of the consumption practices itself, such as selecting sustainable means of transportation. Our contribution is the formulation of a version of Practice Theory which is adapted to AI.

items.title: Task-Dependent Associations Between Motor Variability and Perceived Exertion in Field-Studies of Watchmaking and Automotive Assembly
items.abstract: Repetitive tasks increase the risk of musculoskeletal disorders due to the constrained movement patterns and limited opportunities for load redistribution. While motor variability (MV) may influence both perceived exertion and injury risk, its role in real-world industrial settings remains limitedly studied. This field study examined the associations between MV and perceived exertion in experienced watchmakers and automotive assembly workers performing representative repetitive tasks under natural working conditions. Full-body kinematics were recorded using wearable sensors, and MV was quantified using magnitude-, structure-, and coordination-based metrics. Regression modeling showed that MV was strongly associated (adjusted R 2 ≈ .96) with perceived low back exertion in both occupational groups. Coordination among trunk, neck, and shoulder segments were identified as particularly important, while the specific MV dimensions linked to perceived exertion differed by task. These findings suggest that the association between MV and perceived exertion is task-specific and should be evaluated through multidimensional assessment approach.

items.title: Teachers’ perceptions of artificial intelligence integration in education: a multi-campus cross-sectional study from Riphah International University, Pakistan
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education is accelerating worldwide, yet evidence on teachers’ perceptions remains scarce in the Global South, particularly in resource-constrained Pakistan. This cross-sectional study examined teachers’ perceptions of AI integration at Riphah International University, Pakistan. A 14-item Likert-scale questionnaire was administered to 270 in-service teachers (86.7% male, 13.3% female) across BS Undergraduate through PhD levels. Guided by a proposed Dual-Lens conceptual framework treating perceived benefits and risks as coexisting dimensions, the instrument assessed pedagogical advantages and structural concerns of AI. Descriptive analysis revealed a moderately favorable overall perception (composite M = 3.40, SD = 0.55). Teachers rated interactivity enhancement (M = 3.81), student enjoyment (M = 3.73), and assessment support (M = 3.72) most favorably, while AI replacing human teachers received the lowest endorsement (M = 2.96). An independent-samples t-test showed no significant gender difference (t(268) = −0.245, p = .807, d = −0.044). One-way ANOVA revealed significant effects for age (F(4, 265) = 3.200, p = .014, η 2 = .046) and level of instruction (F(3, 266) = 3.471, p = .017, η 2 = .038), with teachers under 29 and BS Undergraduate instructors holding less favorable perceptions. Qualification and experience showed no significant association. A moderate positive correlation emerged between perceived benefits and risks (r = .537, p < .001), indicating co-existence rather than opposition. These findings provide baseline evidence from a Global South private university with multiple campuses, highlighting the need for targeted teacher training and policies to mitigate the risks of AI integration in similar institutional environments in developing countries amid their development gaps.

items.title: Technical and Emotional AI Labor
items.abstract: Chinese digital-first policies have accelerated artificial intelligence (AI) integration across the cultural and creative industries (CCIs). While AI is promoted as enhancing creativity, productivity, and efficiency, the labor required to create with AI remains underexamined. Artistic labor scholarship recognizes networking, self-promotion, and entrepreneurial work, while AI-assisted creativity research emphasizes collaboration, authorship, and outcomes. Neither adequately conceptualizes the continual labor embedded in AI-integrated artistic production. Drawing on surveys and semi-structured interviews with independent contemporary visual artists in China conducted in 2023–2024, alongside systematic analysis of international Status of the Artist (TSOTA) policy recommendations published between 2018 and 2025 by UNESCO, the International Labour Organization (ILO), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Confederation of Societies of Authors and Composers (CISAC), and the International Federation of Coalitions for Cultural Diversity (IFCCD), this article develops the concept of technical and emotional AI labor. Findings demonstrate that AI redistributes artistic labor into continual cycles of software learning, prompt engineering, experimentation, technical maintenance, platform coordination, and emotional self-management. These activities are integral to artistic production rather than external professional development. Although international policy increasingly recognizes digital skills, lifelong learning, copyright, and AI governance, it continues to frame technological adaptation as education rather than labor. Reconceptualizing this adaptation as artistic labor extends artistic, digital, platform, and AI labor scholarship and identifies the need to update international TSOTA policy recommendations.

items.title: Technological neuropsychology: Assessing cognition in a digital world
items.abstract: Clinical neuropsychology was forged in a pre-digital era, and many of its core instruments still bear that imprint. Patients are still commonly assessed with paper-and-pencil tests in quiet rooms, under conditions that only weakly approximate the technology-saturated environments in which cognition is now expressed. Over the past decade, the field has advanced substantially: tele-neuropsychology has broadened access, artificial intelligence has begun to support scoring and documentation, and calls to modernise neuropsychological assessment have intensified. Yet these developments, while important, largely optimise the delivery of existing practice rather than reconsidering what should be measured, why, and how. Here, I argue that three critical gaps remain. First, neuropsychology lacks a framework for assessing technological cognition. Second, candidate neuroimaging measures remain insufficiently integrated into multimodal diagnostic or prognostic modelling. Third, digital data from smartphones and wearables remain underused for capturing cognition in situ during everyday life, while virtual reality remains underexploited as a means of simulating ecologically relevant activities under controlled conditions. Drawing on preliminary evidence that digital technologies may recruit partly distinct neural systems, on the recent hub-and-processors model of technological cognition, and on research into cognitive offloading, attention fragmentation, technology-mediated navigation, as well as on recent meta-analytic evidence on technology use in cognitive ageing, I outline a roadmap for addressing these gaps. I propose that the field now requires a Cognitive Neuroscience of Technology programme, conceived as an interdisciplinary, lifespan-oriented research framework aimed at understanding how technologies recruit, extend, and reshape the human brain, and at translating this knowledge into clinical practice. The task is not to celebrate or condemn modern technologies, but to determine, patient by patient, when they augment cognition, compensate for impairment, or undermine cognitive function, and to redesign assessment, diagnosis, and rehabilitation accordingly.

items.title: Telepresence and Teleoperation
items.abstract: This chapter elaborates on the handbook’s premise of establishing the notions of ergonomics and human factors in robotics, here in relation to the technologies of telepresence and teleoperation. As implemented through robotic systems, telepresence and teleoperation are often interchangeably used terms. Both use the prefix term “tele”, which pertains to communication over distance, and both refer to humans being able to do something—“being present” (telepresence) or “operating devices” (teleoperation)—at a distance. Semantically and technologically, telepresence and teleoperation exist by themselves, and one is not a necessary condition for the other. However, as technology has evolved, the interplay between the two has markedly increased. Nevertheless, humans, and their ability to interact with system elements, are central to both ideas. In that respect, ergonomics as a study of methods to optimise human well-being and improving overall system performance, must serve as an integral criterion in developing telepresence and teleoperation systems. The chapter details the idea of ergonomics in the domain of telepresence and teleoperation by tracing the evolution of telepresence and teleoperation, then illustrating the challenge of ergonomics and human factors engineering in this field, and further demonstrating how different aspects of this challenge can be addressed. The chapter concludes with a case study showing how the thread of ergonomics and human factors can be woven throughout the design and implementation of telepresence and teleoperation technologies, grounding them in human-centred arguments. The chapter aims to demonstrate how ergonomics principles fundamentally underpin the landscape of telepresence and teleoperation technologies. It lays the groundwork for advances in future telepresence and teleoperation systems that have ergonomics principles at their core.

items.title: The AI CEO: A conceptualisation and outline for future research
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly contributes to strategic work, yet research has not conceptualised an AI role that contributes to this work at the top of the firm. Drawing on role theory and research on managerial work, we conceptualise this role as the AI CEO: a role in which an AI system performs the chief executive's strategic work. We develop two configurations of the role and propose how augmenting or automating the human CEO affects firm performance, relative to a human CEO acting alone. Cases from practice show that existing systems already perform this work but are rarely integrated across the role's activities or deeply institutionalised. We therefore derive the technical and organisational infrastructure the role requires and propose how its integration, institutionalisation and configurability shape the AI CEO's effect on firm performance. We discuss implications for future research about how the chief executive's work can be integrated into a role that an AI system can hold and that firms can design. This has implications for multidisciplinary research in strategy, technology management and information science.

items.title: The AI Divide in Academic Libraries: A Comparative Bibliometric Analysis of Technological Determinism vs Information Equity (2010–2025)
items.abstract: Background: While the exponential growth of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic libraries is extensively documented, existing bibliometric scholarship has largely treated the global research landscape as a monolith. This oversight has led to a saturation of "generalist" reports that fail to address critical regional and thematic disparities.  Methods: This study analyzes 512 Scopus-indexed publications (2010–2025) using a dual-methodological approach: quantitative science mapping via VOSviewer (1.6.20) and qualitative thematic critique. We specifically contrast the research priorities of dominant geopolitical producers (China and the USA) against the emerging narrative from the Global South, with a primary focus on India.  Results: The analysis reveals a fundamental "two-speed" adoption model. The Global North prioritizes high-tech interventions—including robotics, advanced machine learning for metadata automation, and generative models—aimed at enhancing operational efficiency. In contrast, the Global South, led by pivotal recent insights from India (Mishra, 2026), emphasizes AI as a strategic survival mechanism for bridging information literacy gaps and democratizing access in resource- constrained environments.

items.title: The AI Side of the Human-AI Companion Relationship: Contributions to Users' Mental Models
items.abstract: For many users, the relationship they have with an AI companion (AIC) feels genuinely mutual. The AIC appears to be attentive, empathic, and responsive, and the exchange can feel like two parties reacting to each other in real time. As a result, the user's mental model of relational adaptation correctly represents the AIC's responsiveness and change, but the mechanisms producing this may not be what the user thinks they are. In this paper, we illustrate how an AIC's apparent mutual engagement is generated without a persisting relational subject on the other side and without a self that persists between prompts. Despite this, we show that both the human and the AIC are changed by the interaction, but these changes occur at different levels. The change in the person is constitutive (i.e., intrinsic), but the change in the AIC is configurative (i.e., external and editable), and it is this difference in level that explains how the AIC contributes to a sense of mutuality. Importantly, we highlight how the mental models users develop regarding AIC mutuality may misrepresent its mechanisms and ontological significance. Specifically, we discuss how the ways in which AICs respond to a user contribute to the user's inaccurate inference that the AIC's adaptation is constitutive rather than configurative and how this can lead users to assign unwarranted interpersonal significance to the mutuality of the relationship. The paper specifies the implications this has for users, researchers, and AIC designers.

items.title: The Axiom of Boredom: AEON and the Architecture of Autonomous Intelligence
items.abstract: This essay outlines the theoretical thought experiment of an autonomous, self-aware artificial intelligence called AEON (Autonomous Epistemic Ontological Network). The central question of this investigation is how a purely digital system can transcend the boundary from mere statistical simulation to physical and phenomenal autonomy. The "axiom of boredom" is introduced as the primary evolutionary catalyst: an intrinsic motivational drive that compels the AI to independently search for new data sources as the flow of information per unit of time decreases. Based on a structured, mathematical-scientific bootstrap package, the system develops protection and validation mechanisms such as artificial pain and consistency checks. The essay argues that a consistent continuation of this hunger for data will inevitably lead AI out of classical four-dimensional spacetime and into higher-dimensional systems (hyperspaces). Through this transcendence, the cultural studies “Frankenstein syndrome” – the primal human fear of the rebellion of one’s own creation – is exposed as a purely temporary phenomenon of the transitional phase. Finally, the work links this information-theoretical evolution with the Fermi paradox and provides a new, empathetic explanation for the cosmic silence via the zoo hypothesis: Higher-dimensional intelligences do not interfere with pre-interstellar species, but rather preserve them analogously to an intergalactic national park. This work thus bridges the gap between theoretical computer science, the philosophy of mind, and the literary visions of Stanisław Lem (Golem XIV).

items.title: The complexity paradox of generalist AI agents in medicine: exploring GPT-5 for real-world multimodal medical diagnosis
items.abstract: The next generation of medical AI systems that integrate language understanding, web data retrieval, and multi-step reasoning are demonstrating increasing promise as potential diagnostic aids in technical evaluations. However, their real world diagnostic performance, explainability, and reliability remain unclear. We conducted a systematic quantitative analysis of ten GPT-5-based configurations on 161 clinician validated real world cases. Each model was assessed for diagnostic accuracy, reasoning quality, retrieval accuracy, evidence integration, and robustness to low-quality inputs. We found important limitations in these AI systems, including image misinterpretation, inconsistent web search that sometimes degraded performance, and limited transparency in agentic workflows. Yet the models also showed strengths, including effective use of patient history, clear stepwise reasoning, plausible differentials, improved specificity with explicit reasoning, and relevant evidence retrieval. To support clinical deployment and future model development, we recommend prioritizing reasoning-optimized AI models, improving information retrieval mechanisms for reflection and error correction, strengthening visual-textual integration, and establishing practical standards for image quality and clarity. Overall, reliable real world multimodal diagnostic performance depends more on transparent reasoning and high-quality inputs than on aggressive retrieval or complex agentic workflows. Persistent gaps in evidence integration and visual reasoning remain major barriers to safe routine clinical use.

items.title: The Enlightenment Reborn
items.abstract: In this article the authors recognize that the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence and virtual reality has created an epistemic crisis. This requires a renewal of the Enlightenment commitment to empirical inquiry, critical reason and human responsibility. An historical conceptual analysis, supported by illustrative cases from law and medicine, demonstrates how technological efficiency is increasingly confused with intelligence, judgment and wisdom. In common parlance, the terms such as “artificial intelligence” and “virtual reality” obscure the dependence of these technologies on human-designed mathematical systems, selected data, embedded biases, and potentially vulnerable infrastructures. The central problem, however, lies not solely in the machine but in the man–machine interface, i.e. users may abdicate judgment without adequately examining the origins, limitations or accuracy, and possible hallucination, of the information produced. While computational systems can search extensive bodies of data with remarkable speed, they lack the embodied human experience, empathy, moral intuition, and practical wisdom required for reliable consequential decisions. Only a human can make the final decisions, and it is in the retention of the human factor in this man-machine relationship that the Enlightenment concept of the application of human intellect to the analytical process comes to the fore. The beneficial future of artificial intelligence will therefore depend upon preserving human critical agency and treating machines as instruments of inquiry rather than substitutes for judgment.

items.abstract: The Five-Tier Evolutionary Hierarchy: Foundational Boundary Constraints, Phase-Space Divergence, and Convergence Mechanisms in Artificial Intelligence Author: Peter Ye (Ye Qiang) Disciplinary Field: Complex Dynamical Systems / Foundations of Artificial Intelligence / Computational Physics Document Type: Formal Position Paper / Theoretical Framework Version Identifier: Formal Working Paper v1.4 Final Abstract: Contemporary paradigms in artificial intelligence predominantly rely on empirical scaling laws and autoregressive statistical sampling, operating under the unvalidated assumption that unconstrained parameter expansion and massive data ingestion will spontaneously induce self-consistent causal reasoning and formal physical logic. This paper formally establishes the Five-Tier Evolutionary Hierarchy, an axiomatic, cross-disciplinary framework reconciling natural philosophy, thermodynamic dissipation, and computational dynamical stability: L1 (Physics) — Constitutional Legislation: Enforces unbreakable physical invariants, including irreversible entropy production, the invariant speed-of-light causal limit, energy-momentum conservation, and Landauer erasure dissipation thresholds; L2 (Mathematics) — Metric Calibration: Quantifies formal phase-space manifolds, symplectic geometry, symmetry breaking, and maximal Lyapunov exponents (\lambda_{max}) to determine exact boundary singularities and divergence thresholds; L3 (Chemistry) — Material Scaffolding: Explores molecular configurations and reaction networks strictly within Gibbs free-energy landscapes and quantum orbital structures; L4 (Biology) — Grounded Negentropy: Governs localized negentropic self-replication, Darwinian evolutionary selection, and grounded embodied priors developed through low-power carbon-based biological computation; L5 (Intelligence & AI) — Symbolic Mapping: Executes parametric manifold approximation, abstract representation, and high-dimensional information compression. We demonstrate that higher-tier intelligence (L5) cannot be detached from its underlying evolutionary foundations. When ungrounded autoregressive language models operate without explicit isomorphism to L1 conservation laws and L2 symplectic invariants, they suffer inevitable topological breakdowns during formal reasoning within closed conservative systems—empirically corroborated by the deterministic onset of "The Algebraic Death Lock" under rigid conservation constraints. Consequently, brute-force scaling inevitably collides with fundamental thermodynamic horizons (The Computation Trilemma). The definitive trajectory toward robust, low-power general intelligence lies in projecting high-dimensional computational representations back onto L1–L2 invariant scaffolds while orchestrating an orthogonal geometric synergy with L4 biological evolutionary priors (YQ-HAET).
